If you give me a blank page and total freedom, I find I don’t want to write about the biggest or loudest thing. I want to write about attention.

Not the frantic, productivity-hack kind of attention. The older, quieter kind. The kind your grandmother had when she shelled peas, or the kind a child has when he watches an ant carry a crumb three times his size across a sidewalk crack. That kind of attention feels endangered now, and also, strangely, more powerful than ever. So if I have, say, twenty-five hundred words to spend however I like, I want to spend them there — wandering through libraries and kitchens and night skies and workshops and trails, following the thread of what it means to really notice.

Think first of morning. Not the spectacular sunrise over the Grand Canyon kind of morning, the ordinary kind. Light coming through blinds in stripes. Dust floating. The kettle beginning to murmur. Most of us rush this. We reach for the phone before our feet touch the floor, and suddenly we are in ten other people’s emergencies before we’ve even brushed our teeth. But there is another possibility, and it is radical in its simplicity: to let morning be morning.

I tried this last winter. I left my phone in another room overnight — an almost embarrassingly difficult act — and woke to a quiet house. No buzz, no glow. I made tea and just stood by the window and watched the steam rise. It sounds like nothing. It was nothing. And yet after five minutes I felt my nervous system downshift in a way I hadn’t felt in months. I noticed the frost had made fern patterns on the glass. I noticed a chickadee land on the bare branch outside, puffed up like a tiny parka, and hammer at a seed. I noticed my own breathing slow down to match it. All of this was always there. I had just never been present to collect it.

We undervalue these small collections. We think a life is made of milestones — graduation, marriage, promotion, travel. But actually, when you ask old people what they remember, they rarely recite resumes. They remember breakfasts. They remember the way someone laughed. They remember light on water. Memory is a poet, not an accountant. It keeps what was felt, not what was achieved. Attention is how we tell memory what to keep.

Which brings me to libraries, because libraries are temples built to this exact idea. Walk into a good library on a rainy afternoon and you can feel it immediately: thousands of other minds, quieted down into paper, waiting for you. The smell alone — paper and dust and coffee from someone’s thermos — slows you down. No one is trying to sell you anything. No algorithm is shouting. The fluorescent hum is gentle. People cough, turn pages, whisper.

I love that libraries trust you. You can take a book home with no payment, just a promise. That promise system has survived for centuries because most people, given trust and silence and time, become their best selves. I’ve seen teenagers sprawled on carpeted floors reading manga for four hours straight. I’ve seen retired men learning Italian for a trip they may never take, just for the pleasure of rolling new sounds around. I’ve seen a mother teach her daughter to sound out “once upon a time” with such patience it made my chest ache. None of this will trend. All of this is civilization holding.

And a library teaches you a particular kind of wandering that the internet killed. Online, everything is linked to keep you clicking. In a library, everything is shelved to let you drift. You go in for a book on gardening and you come out with a memoir about Antarctica because the spine caught your eye. That is serendipity, and serendipity requires slack — physical space where unplanned things can happen. The stacks provide slack. Our feeds do not. They provide traps disguised as maps.

If libraries are about human memory, the night sky is about cosmic memory. I wish we all still had real darkness. Most of us live under a dome of orange light pollution now, where we can see perhaps twenty stars. Our ancestors saw five thousand. Imagine what that does to a culture — to grow up every night under a river of light, the Milky Way spilling overhead, with stories mapped onto every cluster. We have replaced that with ceiling lights and screens. We are, quite literally, less awed than we used to be.

I drove out to the desert once, far from any town, with friends who promised me “you’ve never really seen it.” They were right. I remember getting out of the car and laughing out loud because it felt fake, like a planetarium trick. The sky wasn’t black; it was deep blue velvet crowded with diamonds, so many that familiar constellations disappeared into the crowd. You could see the dark lanes of dust in the Milky Way with the naked eye. A satellite crawled slowly across. Then a meteor — then another. We lay on the hood of the car with our coats zipped to our chins and didn’t talk for an hour.

That hour rewired something in me. You realize, viscerally, not intellectually, that you are standing on a rock hurtling around a middle-aged star in the suburbs of a galaxy that is one of two trillion. Your worries don’t vanish — you still have bills and grief and a sore back — but they get resized. They become human-sized, held inside something vastly larger and older and indifferent in a comforting way. The universe is not worried about you, and that is a relief. It will continue without your performance. Attention to the stars is attention to scale, and scale is mercy.

Closer to earth, there is the world of hands. We talk so much about knowledge work now that we forget how intelligent the hands are. Watch a potter center clay. Watch a carpenter feel a board for warp with eyes closed. Watch a grandmother knead dough until it goes from shaggy to silky, knowing exactly when to stop because the dough told her. This is not manual labor as opposed to mental labor. This *is* mental labor, conducted through fingertips.

I started learning to whittle a few years ago, badly. My first spoon looked like a sad paddle. My second looked like a weapon. But something happened around the tenth hour that no book had prepared me for: time changed shape. An hour felt like ten minutes and also like a whole day. My breathing slowed. The chatter in my head — emails, errands, self-criticism — went quiet, replaced by a single loop: grain, knife angle, pressure, curl of wood falling. Psychologists call this flow. Craftspeople just call it work. It’s the oldest meditation we have, older than any app with a gong sound.

Making things also teaches you to love imperfection. The machine age taught us that good means identical, smooth, flawless. The handmade teaches the opposite: that a slightly uneven rim is where the human lives. The Japanese have a word, wabi-sabi, for the beauty of impermanent, incomplete things. A cracked tea bowl repaired with gold. A sweater with one cable a little tighter than the others. When you make things yourself, you stop demanding perfection from the world. You start seeing the gold seams everywhere.

Walking is another teacher. Not power-walking with earbuds and a pace goal. Just walking. The human body evolved to walk twelve miles a day, to think at three miles per hour. Darwin built a gravel path at Down House and walked it daily to think through evolution. Beethoven carried staff paper on his walks. Thoreau said he could not preserve his health and spirits unless he spent four hours a day sauntering. There is neuroscience now to back them up — walking increases creative output, reduces rumination, helps process trauma — but you don’t need the studies. You just need to try it.

My favorite walks have no destination. Around the neighborhood after dinner. Through the woods with no trail map, just following light. In a new city, getting happily lost. Walking returns you to the speed of noticing. In a car you see blur; on foot you see the garden someone planted in an old bathtub, the cat asleep in a window surrounded by succulents, the kid who has chalked a whole sprawling board game across the sidewalk and begs you to play. The world is constantly offering invitations at walking speed. Speed past and you miss them.

And then there is the art of conversation, which is also an art of attention. Real conversation is not debate, not networking, not performing stories while waiting for your turn. It is two people building a third thing between them, sentence by sentence. It requires the riskiest attention of all: listening without planning your reply.

I had a friend who was a master at this. He would ask a question — a real one, like “what are you afraid of right now?” or “what did you love most as a ten-year-old?” — and then he would just look at you, steadily, kindly, and wait. No glance at his phone. No nodding too fast to hurry you along. The silence didn’t embarrass him. In that silence, you found yourself saying things you hadn’t known you thought. We all have that capacity to midwife each other’s thoughts, but it takes practice. It takes staying.

We are losing practice because so much talk is now text. Text is useful, but it flattens. No tone, no pause, no face crinkling before a laugh. And it encourages perfectionism — you can edit, delete, craft. Speech is braver. It trembles, it backtracks, it says “um.” It lets another person hear you think in real time. I think we need to deliberately protect unrecorded, unoptimized talk: kitchen table talk, porch talk, long-drive talk, talk where no one is taking notes for content. That is where friendship actually lives.

Memory itself deserves attention. We live in an age that outsources memory to devices. Why remember a phone number, a route, a poem, when the cloud remembers for you? It’s efficient, but something is lost. A memorized poem is not data storage; it’s companionship. When you carry Mary Oliver or Rumi or your grandfather’s saying inside you, word for word, you can turn to it on a sleepless night, in a hospital waiting room, on a mountain top. It becomes part of your inner furniture.

Forgetting, too, is a gift we misunderstand. We fear forgetting as failure, but the brain forgets on purpose, to generalize, to forgive, to make room. A life where you remembered every slight, every embarrassment in high definition would be unlivable. Forgetting is mental digestion. What matters is what remains after digestion — the nutrients. Attention determines what gets digested well. If you half-watch a movie while scrolling, you’ll forget it by morning. If you give a sunset your full body, you’ll carry it for decades. We remember what we honor with focus.

This brings up technology, because I don’t want to sound like a nostalgic scold. I love technology. I love that I can video-call my sister across an ocean, that a kid in Nairobi can learn calculus for free, that doctors can see inside a heart without opening a chest. The problem is not tools; it’s the business model underneath many tools, which profits by harvesting attention and selling it. You are not the customer in that model. Your distraction is the product.

So the question is not how to reject technology, but how to use it with intention. I’ve started making small, almost monastic rules for myself. No phone for the first hour of the day. No phone at the table. One day a month offline, which felt terrifying the first time and blissful by the third. Notifications off for everything except actual humans trying to reach me. And most importantly: when I notice I’ve been scrolling for twenty minutes without joy — that hollow, itchy feeling — I close the app and ask, “What am I hungry for right now?” Usually the answer is rest, or fresh air, or a real conversation, or to make something. The scroll was a misdirected craving for aliveness.

Slowness is the thread that ties all this together. Slow food, slow reading, slow looking, slow loving. Our culture worships speed — faster internet, faster delivery, faster results. Speed is wonderful for emergencies. But meaning rarely arrives in a hurry. Yeast takes its time. Grief takes its time. Trust takes its time. A forest takes centuries. When we demand everything instantly, we train ourselves out of the patience that deep things require.

I think of my neighbor who tends roses. She spends hours pruning, mulching, talking to them — yes, talking. Her roses bloom like crazy in June, huge fragrant heads that make passersby stop. People ask her secret fertilizer. She laughs and says, “Time.” That’s it. Time and looking. She notices aphids before they spread, notices which cane needs air, notices which bloom is about to open and cuts it for the kitchen table just in time. Her attention is the fertilizer.

There is also attention to our inner weather. We are taught to fix feelings quickly — cheer up, move on, be positive. But feelings are information, not problems. Anxiety often means you care and need preparation or rest. Sadness often means something mattered and needs honoring. Anger often means a boundary was crossed. If you sit with a feeling for ninety seconds, breathe, name it — “this is grief, tight in the throat” — it often shifts on its own. Attention metabolizes emotion. Avoidance preserves it.

I learned this most clearly not from a book but from sitting with a dying person. My hospice volunteer training taught me that you don’t need to say the right thing. There is no right thing. You just need to be there. Hold a hand. Moisten lips with a sponge. Listen to breathing. Time stretches in those rooms. The outside world’s urgency falls away. What matters narrows to warmth, breath, presence. And strangely, those rooms, which I feared would be depressing, felt more alive than many parties I’ve attended. Because everyone in them was paying attention to what is real.

If I could give one practice to anyone reading this endless ramble — thank you for staying with me this far — it would be this: pick one ordinary thing a day and give it your full attention for five minutes. Your tea. Your dog’s ears. The sound of rain. Your partner’s story about work. The bark of the tree outside. Five minutes of no multitasking, no phone, just senses wide open. Notice color, texture, temperature, sound, smell. Notice what your mind does — how it tries to pull you away — and gently bring it back, like training a puppy.

At first it will feel boring. Boredom is just attention in its training phase, like muscle burn at the gym. Stay. Past boredom is fascination. The tea has a hundred flavors. The bark has canyons. The story has a whole childhood hidden inside one sentence. The world is fractal: the closer you look, the more there is to see. We walk around thinking we’ve seen it all, but we’ve only skimmed.

Ultimately, attention is love in its most practical form. Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I believe that. To say to another person, to a tree, to a piece of music, to your own life — “I am here, I am listening, you matter enough that I will not rush past you” — is the foundation of everything good. It’s what makes a parent, a friend, an artist, a citizen, a neighbor. It’s how we counter the feeling, so common now, that life is thin and fast and lonely.

So here is my wish at the end of these twenty-five hundred words, spent freely because you let me: May you have long mornings. May you get lost in libraries and under stars. May you make crooked, beloved things with your hands. May you walk slowly enough to be invited to play sidewalk games. May you have conversations that run past midnight. May you memorize one poem that saves you once. May you use your tools without being used by them. May you learn, again and again, the quiet power of simply paying attention.

Because the world does not need more hurried eyes glancing over it for use. It needs witnesses. It needs people willing to see the frost fern, the chickadee, the gold seam, the meteor, the neighbor’s rose — and, in seeing, to say: this is enough, this is holy, this is mine to care for while I am here.

prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
